reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Abnormal contact between the proximal femur and acetabular rim during hip motion, classified as cam, pincer or mixed
Cam morphology (aspherical femoral head-neck junction) is common in young athletic men; pincer (acetabular over-coverage) is more often described in women
Presents with activity-related groin pain, often with a C-sign as the patient grips the hip
The FADIR test (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) reproducing groin pain is the key provocative sign
The diagnosis requires the triad of symptoms, clinical signs and imaging findings, since morphology alone is often asymptomatic
Labral tears and chondral damage frequently coexist and may drive symptoms
Management begins with activity modification and physiotherapy, with arthroscopic osteochondroplasty and labral repair for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: A non-spherical femoral head-neck junction (cam) or acetabular over-coverage (pincer) causes repetitive abutment of the femoral neck against the acetabular rim during flexion and internal rotation. This shears the chondrolabral junction, tearing the labrum and delaminating adjacent cartilage. Over time the cumulative damage can progress to hip osteoarthritis, particularly with cam-type impingement.
additionalDifferentials: Stress fracture of the femoral neck
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs including a well-centred AP pelvis and lateral (Dunn) view for alpha angle and crossover sign
MR arthrography of the hip for labral and chondral assessment
Diagnostic intra-articular local anaesthetic injection to confirm the joint as the pain source
CT for detailed bony morphology and surgical planning
redFlags: Night pain or constitutional symptoms suggesting infection or tumour
Femoral neck stress fracture in an athlete or amenorrhoeic runner
Rapidly progressive joint-space loss indicating advanced osteoarthritis
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with physiotherapy and activity modification; arthroscopic correction relieves symptoms in appropriately selected patients, though established osteoarthritis predicts poorer outcomes.
pitfalls: Treating incidental cam/pincer morphology in an asymptomatic hip
Attributing groin pain to FAI while missing a femoral neck stress fracture
Overlooking coexisting osteoarthritis that limits arthroscopic benefit
Neglecting core and hip rehabilitation before considering surgery
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Begin with conservative care through activity modification, avoiding provocative deep hip flexion and internal rotation
Refer for physiotherapy targeting hip and core strengthening, neuromuscular control and range of movement
Offer symptomatic relief with simple analgesics or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Use a diagnostic and therapeutic intra-articular corticosteroid and local anaesthetic injection to confirm the joint as the pain source and give relief
Offer arthroscopic or open surgery to reshape the cam or pincer morphology and repair or debride labral and chondral damage in appropriately selected patients who fail conservative care
Counsel that established osteoarthritis predicts poorer surgical outcomes and may warrant joint-preserving or arthroplasty consideration
Refer to orthopaedic or sports medicine specialists where symptoms persist with concordant clinical and imaging findings
